USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: The US should follow through on the threatened tariff escalation—raising the $200bn tranche from 10% to 25% and beginning the process to tariff the remaining ~$300bn of Chinese imports. This maintains maximum leverage while talks are ongoing and signals that backsliding on commitments will carry real costs. The US should simultaneously keep the negotiating channel open but refuse to lower tariffs until China enacts verifiable structural reforms.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is moderate-to-elevated (threat_score +0.35). The $419bn trade deficit (BBC, 2019-05-08) represents a persistent structural imbalance. China's state subsidies, forced technology transfer, and IP theft (Fox Business; USC Annenberg) threaten US competitiveness in the industries of the future—AI, cloud computing, robotics, green tech (USC Annenberg). However, the US economy is not in existential danger: the Dow is up ~11% YTD in 2019 (BBC), and the US consumer/labor market remains relatively strong. The threat is real but manageable.

The action_score of -1.0 (maximal escalation via tariffs) is justified by several factors. First, the US has significant leverage: China's export-dependent economy is more vulnerable to tariff disruption than the US consumer economy, and supply chains are already shifting to other countries (Fox Business, Graham: tariffs 'make other countries a cheaper place to do business'). Second, this is described as 'the best chance in my lifetime to get China to change their cheating ways' (Sen. Graham, Fox Business). Third, White House adviser Kudlow acknowledged 'both sides will suffer' but the asymmetry favors the US in the medium term. Fourth, the USC analysis confirms the negotiations are 'not principally about current buying and selling, but rather about the most important and potentially profitable industries of the future'—this is a structural contest where short-term pain is justified. Fifth, China has already retaliated with tariffs on $110bn of US goods and new levies on $60bn (USC Annenberg), so the cost of inaction is continued erosion of US competitive position. The Wilson Center historical analysis warns of unintended consequences of protectionism, but the current leverage position is favorable and the structural issues demand resolution.
key_factors: China's state subsidies, forced tech transfer, IP theft threaten US tech leadership (USC Annenberg, Fox Business)
US market resilience: Dow up ~11% YTD 2019, providing economic buffer (BBC)
Supply chain shift away from China creates leverage (Fox Business/Graham)
Negotiations focus on future industries—AI, cloud, robotics—not just current trade (USC Annenberg)
China already retaliated on $110bn US goods + $60bn new levies, showing willingness to escalate (USC Annenberg)
IMF cut 2019 global growth forecast citing US-China tensions (BBC)

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should announce retaliatory tariffs on the remaining ~$60 billion of US goods not yet covered, matching the US escalation on $200 billion (raised from 10% to 25%) and the threatened additional $300 billion. Retaliation signals resolve, preserves negotiating leverage, and rallies domestic support without closing the door to talks.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat score of +0.55 reflects the severe and escalating nature of the trade war as of early June 2019. The US has already imposed tariffs on $250 billion of Chinese goods and raised the rate on $200 billion from 10% to 25% (BBC, 2019-05-08). Trump has further threatened tariffs on 'essentially all remaining imports from China, valued at approximately $300 billion' (Fox Business, 2019-05-12). This threatens China's export economy, which is central to GDP growth and employment in export hubs. The USC analysis notes that the dispute is fundamentally about 'the most important and potentially profitable industries of the future — AI, cloud computing, robotics, green tech' (Annenberg USC), meaning the stakes go beyond trade balances to China's industrial upgrading goals (Made in China 2025). China has already retaliated on $110 billion of US goods and announced new levies on $60 billion (BBC; Annenberg USC), but the asymmetry in tariff coverage ($250bn US vs $110bn China) means China still has room to match. The action score of -1.0 (maximal retaliation stance) reflects the judgment that China must demonstrate it will not be coerced into concessions under threat. Conceding now — before the US has offered meaningful structural compromises on entity-list actions or technology restrictions — would signal weakness and invite further escalation. Retaliation preserves leverage for eventual negotiations while rallying domestic nationalist support. The risk of further US escalation (the $300 billion threat) is real, but capitulation carries greater long-term strategic cost. China should retaliate now and signal willingness to negotiate if the US de-escalates.
key_factors: US raised tariffs on $200bn of Chinese goods from 10% to 25% in May 2019
Trump threatened tariffs on remaining ~$300bn of Chinese imports
China already retaliated on $110bn but asymmetry remains ($250bn US vs $110bn China)
Dispute centers on future tech industries (AI, cloud, robotics) critical to Made in China 2025
IMF cut 2019 global growth forecast citing US-China tensions
China's export economy and employment in export hubs at risk
US demands include structural changes (IP protection, market access, end forced tech transfer) that go beyond trade balance
